Suricata and an ML flow classifier

1. HIKARI-2021: encrypted attacks

The attacks are HTTPS brute force and scans on port 443. Suricata's rules match on content, and with TLS there is none to match. The model uses packet counts, sizes and timing, which encryption leaves intact.

The model's precision on HIKARI is only 48.5%: it also flags 7,784 benign flows. check_duplicates.py lists attack flows that also appear as Benign with identical features, which limits how precise any model can be here.

2. TLS inspection lab: the same attacks encrypted and decrypted

We generated HIKARI-style traffic against a WordPress site behind an nginx TLS terminator and recorded both the encrypted side and the plaintext hop behind it. Suricata sees nothing on the encrypted side and most of the attacks once the traffic is decrypted.

* Scored on its own held-out 20% of the flows; the other columns use all flows. The model trained on HIKARI-2021 flags almost nothing in the lab, so a model has to be trained on the traffic of the network it protects.

3. CSE-CIC-IDS2018: plaintext attacks

Here the attacks are mostly readable, so Suricata is back in play. It catches payload attacks such as XSS; the model catches volumetric and slow attacks such as DoS and brute force.

4. The model as a filter behind Suricata

An alert is kept only if the model also flags the flow. On the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 held-out flows this removes 5,354 of Suricata's 5,355 false alerts and loses 32 of its 293 true alerts.

Offline replays of recorded captures; real-time load, memory and packet drops were not measured. CSE-CIC-IDS2018 labels come from documented attacker addresses, not per-flow ground truth.
